summary:
Texas is a community-property state, and every tracing engagement starts from Texas Family Code §3.003: (a) property possessed by either spouse during or on dissolution of marriage is presumed to be community property, and (b) the degree of proof necessary to establish that property is separate is clear and convincing evidence — the highest civil standard, defined in Tex. Fam. Code §101.007 as proof producing "a firm belief or conviction" of the truth of the allegation. Separate property (§3.001) is what a spouse owned before marriage, acquired during marriage by gift, devise, or descent, or received as a personal-injury recovery (except lost earning capacity). Character is fixed by the inception-of-title doctrine: an asset takes its character at the moment the right or claim to it first arises, and that character does not change through later mutations of form — sale proceeds, reinvestments, and exchanges remain separate if (and only if) the claimant "clearly traces the original property through all of its mutations" (Norris v. Vaughan, 260 S.W.2d 676 (Tex. 1953); Estate of Hanau v. Hanau). But when separate and community funds are "so commingled as to defy resegregation and identification," the community presumption prevails and the separate claim is lost (Tarver v. Tarver, 394 S.W.2d 780 (Tex. 1965); McKinley v. McKinley, 496 S.W.2d 540, 543 (Tex. 1973)). Commingling alone does not destroy separate character — failure of proof does; courts such as Welder v. Welder, 794 S.W.2d 420 (Tex. App.—Corpus Christi 1990), and Zagorski v. Zagorski, 116 S.W.3d 309 (Tex. App.—Houston [14th Dist.] 2003, pet. denied), upheld multi-million-dollar separate characterizations of heavily transacted accounts because adequate records plus expert tracing schedules carried the burden.

The forensic accountant's toolkit consists of judicially accepted tracing methods applied to a chronological, transaction-by-transaction reconstruction of each account. (1) Community-out-first (the Sibley rule): where an account holds both estates, the spouse is treated like a trustee who is presumed to spend the community (trust analogy: the trustee's "own" funds) first, so withdrawals deplete the community layer and separate dollars "sink to the bottom" — Sibley v. Sibley, 286 S.W.2d 657, 659 (Tex. Civ. App.—Dallas 1955, writ dism'd). (2) Minimum sum balance (lowest intermediate balance): separate character survives to the extent the running balance never dips below the proven separate contribution; if the balance does dip, the separate component is permanently reduced to that low-water mark and can only be replenished by new, provably separate deposits — illustrated by Snider v. Snider, 613 S.W.2d 8 (Tex. Civ. App.—Dallas 1981) ($29,642.45 of a $35,809.80 balance traced because the balance never fell below the separate contributions), and Hill v. Hill, 971 S.W.2d 153 (Tex. App.—Amarillo 1998, no pet.). (3) Clearinghouse: the account is a mere conduit — identifiable separate deposits go in and identical or near-identical amounts promptly come out to buy the disputed asset, so the account's other activity is irrelevant. (4) Identical sum inference: a single separate deposit followed by a withdrawal of the identical sum supports the inference that the withdrawn funds were the separate money — applied by the Texas Supreme Court in McKinley (the original $9,500 CD traced as separate; the $953.81 of accumulated interest was community, since in Texas income from separate property during marriage is community). (5) Pro rata / proportional approaches: when an asset is purchased with mixed funds, the estates own it pro rata in proportion to their contributions (Gleich v. Bongio, 99 S.W.2d 881 (Tex. 1937)), and some practitioners use pro-rata allocation of withdrawals as an alternative account convention where community-out-first is unworkable.

What the expert actually presents is a tracing schedule: a chronological spreadsheet of every deposit and withdrawal, with columns for date, payee/source, deposit, withdrawal, the characterization of each transaction, and — critically — three running balances: community balance, separate balance, and total (which must tie to the bank statement every period). Each deposit is characterized from source documents (payroll = community; inheritance wire = separate; interest = community even on separate principal); each withdrawal is applied community-out-first, invading separate only when community is exhausted; the ending separate balance is the traced separate claim, cross-checked against the minimum-balance analysis. This "tracing sheet" format traces to 1970s Texas practice built directly on Sibley and Farrow v. Farrow, 238 S.W.2d 255 (Tex. Civ. App.—Austin 1951) ("a dollar is a dollar" — money is fungible and traced by amount, not serial number), and courts admit these schedules as summaries under the evidence rules when the underlying records are produced (Welder). The failure modes the expert must anticipate: gaps in statements, unexplained deposits (presumed community), and balances that hit zero — which wipes out the separate layer forever.
key_points: Tex. Fam. Code §3.003(a): property possessed by either spouse during or on dissolution of marriage is presumed community; §3.003(b): rebuttal requires clear and convincing evidence (firm belief or conviction, §101.007) — a higher bar than preponderance, but lower than beyond reasonable doubt.

Tex. Fam. Code §3.001 separate property: (1) owned or claimed before marriage; (2) acquired during marriage by gift, devise, or descent; (3) personal-injury recovery except lost earning capacity. Unique Texas rule: income earned during marriage on separate property (interest, dividends, rents, royalties from produced-and-sold minerals per Norris v. Vaughan) is COMMUNITY.

Inception-of-title doctrine: character is fixed when the right or claim first arises (e.g., contract date for realty, policy date, pre-marriage account opening) and never changes by later events; mutations (sale proceeds, reinvestments, exchanges) keep separate character IF clearly traced — Norris v. Vaughan, 260 S.W.2d 676, 679 (Tex. 1953): claimant must 'trace and clearly identify' property through all mutations; see also Estate of Hanau v. Hanau, 730 S.W.2d 663 (Tex. 1987).

Commingling rule: if separate and community are 'so commingled as to defy resegregation and identification,' the community presumption prevails — Tarver v. Tarver, 394 S.W.2d 780 (Tex. 1965); McKinley v. McKinley, 496 S.W.2d 540, 543 (Tex. 1973). Commingling is a failure-of-proof doctrine, not automatic forfeiture: with complete records, even a heavily transacted account can be traced (Welder v. Welder, 794 S.W.2d 420; Zagorski v. Zagorski, 116 S.W.3d 309 — $2,057,524.20 of premarital funds and mutations traced by clear and convincing evidence despite commingled community interest income).

Method 1 — Community-Out-First (Sibley rule): Sibley v. Sibley, 286 S.W.2d 657 (Tex. Civ. App.—Dallas 1955, writ dism'd) — the spouse holding mixed funds is analogized to a trustee, and equity presumes community funds are withdrawn first, leaving separate funds in the account ('separate dollars sink to the bottom'). Reaffirmed in Horlock v. Horlock (1976): 'where a bank account contains both community and separate monies, it is presumed that community monies are drawn out first.' Mechanics: apply every withdrawal against the running community balance until exhausted, then against separate; deposits are layered by characterized source.

Method 2 — Minimum Sum Balance (lowest intermediate balance rule): separate character survives to the extent the account balance never drops below the cumulative proven separate contribution; any dip permanently ratchets the separate component down to the low-water mark (replenishment requires new separate deposits, not community ones). Snider v. Snider, 613 S.W.2d 8 (Tex. Civ. App.—Dallas 1981): $27,642 premarital balance + $10,000 separate deposit after withdrawals reduced it to $19,642 → separate floor of $29,642; balance never fell below that, so $29,642.45 of the $35,809.80 date-of-death balance was separate. Also Hill v. Hill, 971 S.W.2d 153 (Tex. App.—Amarillo 1998, no pet.).

Method 3 — Clearinghouse: the account serves as a mere conduit — identifiable separate deposits in, identical (or nearly identical) amounts out shortly after to acquire the disputed asset; the surrounding account noise doesn't defeat tracing because the flow itself is documented dollar-for-dollar.

Method 4 — Identical Sum Inference: single deposit of proven separate funds followed by a withdrawal of the identical sum supports the inference the withdrawal was those separate funds. Applied by the Texas Supreme Court in McKinley v. McKinley, 496 S.W.2d 540 (Tex. 1973): husband's premarital $9,500 traced into successive CDs as separate; the $953.81 of interest accrued during marriage was community (account grew $9,500 → $10,453.81).

Method 5 — Pro rata approaches: (a) asset-level: when purchase money is part separate/part community, the estates own the asset as tenants in common pro rata to contributions — Gleich v. Bongio, 99 S.W.2d 881 (Tex. 1937) (e.g., Sibley: farm found 11% community / 89% separate); (b) account-level pro-rata allocation of each withdrawal is a fallback convention some experts present as a sensitivity alongside community-out-first.

Fungibility principle: Farrow v. Farrow, 238 S.W.2d 255 (Tex. Civ. App.—Austin 1951) — 'a dollar is a dollar'; money is traced by amount and character, not by identifying the specific bills; this is what makes spreadsheet tracing legally sufficient.

The expert's tracing schedule: a chronological ledger, one row per transaction, columns typically = Date | Description/Source or Payee | Document ref (statement/check no.) | Deposit | Withdrawal | Character of transaction (SP/CP/unknown) | Running Community Balance | Running Separate Balance | Running Total Balance. Total must reconcile to bank statements every period; unexplained deposits default to community (the presumption cuts against the claimant); each withdrawal applied community-out-first; ending separate balance = traced separate claim, corroborated by a minimum-balance check. Admissible as a summary of voluminous records with expert testimony (Welder v. Welder).

Practice realities: burden is on the claiming spouse; testimony alone ('that money came from my inheritance') without documentary tracing is generally insufficient; gaps in statements can sever the chain; a zero or near-zero balance destroys the separate layer permanently; tracing supports characterization, which is distinct from reimbursement claims (Tex. Fam. Code §3.402) that compensate one estate for benefits conferred on another.

Verification sources: Texas statutes (statutes.capitol.texas.gov, Fam. Code ch. 3); Sibley opinion on CourtListener; State Bar of Texas article on the development of tracing commingled funds (texasbar.com ContentID=35144, history of Stewart's tracing sheets built on Farrow + Sibley); Greg Enos, 'The Basics of Tracing' (2024); Kathryn J. Murphy, 'Tracing and Characterization of Property' (gbfamilylaw.com); Wilson Legal Group method pages (minimum sum balance, clearinghouse/identical sum); FindLaw/vLex Zagorski opinion; Justia Norris v. Vaughan.
terminology: Community presumption — the §3.003(a) default that all property possessed during or on dissolution of marriage is community.
Clear and convincing evidence — §3.003(b) rebuttal standard: proof producing a firm belief or conviction (Tex. Fam. Code §101.007).
Characterization — classifying each asset/dollar as separate property (SP) or community property (CP).
Inception of title — character fixes at the moment the right or claim to the asset first arises and never changes thereafter.
Mutation — a change in the form of separate property (cash → stock → house); character survives mutation if traced.
Tracing — establishing by documents the origin and every subsequent movement of separate funds through all mutations.
Commingling — mixing separate and community funds in one account or asset; fatal only when it 'defies resegregation and identification.'
Resegregation — the analytical re-separation of commingled funds back into their SP and CP components.
Community-out-first rule (Sibley rule) — presumption that withdrawals from a mixed account consume community funds before separate funds.
Trustee analogy — Sibley's equitable rationale: the spouse holding mixed funds is like a trustee presumed to spend his own (community) funds before trust (separate) funds.
Minimum sum balance / lowest intermediate balance rule (LIBR) — separate character survives up to the lowest balance the account hit after the separate deposit.
Separate-property floor / low-water mark — the minimum balance that caps the surviving separate claim; ratchets down on dips, never back up without new SP deposits.
Clearinghouse method — tracing through an account used as a mere conduit: separate money in, identical amount out to the target asset.
Identical sum inference — inference that a withdrawal equal to a prior separate deposit consists of those separate funds (McKinley).
Pro rata ownership — mixed-funds purchase makes the estates tenants in common in proportion to contributions (Gleich v. Bongio).
'A dollar is a dollar' — Farrow principle that money is fungible and traced by amount/character, not physical identity.
Tracing schedule / tracing sheets — the expert's chronological ledger with running community, separate, and total balance columns tying to bank statements.
Unexplained deposit — a deposit whose source cannot be documented; defaults to community under the presumption.
Sole-management community property — community property one spouse would own if single (Tex. Fam. Code §3.102); often confused with separate property by laypeople.
Reimbursement claim (§3.402) — equitable money claim between marital estates; the remedy when tracing/characterization fails or one estate enhanced another — distinct from tracing.
Doctrine of onerous vs. gratuitous acquisition — property acquired by labor/effort during marriage is community; acquired by gift/devise/descent is separate.
demo_ideas: Centerpiece — 'Layered reservoir' chart of the commingled account: a stacked area/step chart over time where the separate layer is drawn at the BOTTOM (visually literalizing Sibley's 'separate sinks to the bottom, community is drawn off the top') and the community layer floats above it. Every withdrawal visibly erodes the community band first; only when the total line cuts into the bottom layer does separate shrink. A forensic accountant will instantly recognize this as community-out-first made visual.

Minimum-balance 'ratchet line': overlay a horizontal (stepwise) 'separate property floor' that only moves DOWN when the total balance dips below it (permanent impairment, annotated with the date and the dollars of separate character destroyed) and steps UP only on new documented separate deposits. Show the low-water-mark event as a highlighted 'invasion event' marker with a callout: 'Balance fell to $19,642 on 3/14/2019 — separate claim permanently reduced from $27,642 to $19,642.'

Interactive timeline scrubber: drag across the account history and watch the running SP/CP split recompute transaction-by-transaction, with a live ticker of Community Balance / Separate Balance / Total that always ties to the bank statement balance — the tie-out is the credibility feature experts care about.

Method toggle for sensitivity analysis: switch the same account between Community-Out-First, Pro Rata Withdrawals, and Minimum Sum Balance and show the resulting separate claim change (e.g., $412,300 vs $377,900 vs $389,642) — mirrors how a testifying expert bulletproofs an opinion against cross-examination.

Exhibit-grade tracing schedule view: a virtualized ledger table (Date | Source/Payee | Doc Ref | Deposit | Withdrawal | Character | CP Balance | SP Balance | Total) where clicking any row highlights the corresponding point on the chart, and clicking a deposit shows its 'source document' chip (inheritance wire, payroll ACH, interest credit). Flag unexplained deposits in amber that auto-default to community.

Mutation flow / Sankey diagram: trace an inheritance through its mutations — $250k bequest → brokerage account → sale proceeds → down payment on ranch — each node stamped with the inception-of-title date and the document that links it, with a 'chain-of-title integrity' indicator that breaks (turns red) if any link lacks a document.

Commingling stress meter: a gauge or annotation that flags when the account approaches 'defies resegregation' territory — e.g., statement gaps, unexplained deposits above a threshold, or a zero-balance event that wipes the separate layer — echoing Tarver/McKinley language a practitioner would quote in a report.

Clearinghouse animation: for conduit transactions, animate the identical sum entering and leaving within days (deposit $85,000 / withdrawal $85,000), dimming all unrelated account noise to demonstrate why the surrounding activity is irrelevant.

Burden-of-proof framing in the UI: label the output not as 'separate property' but as 'traced separate claim, supportable by clear and convincing evidence,' with a per-dollar confidence tier (documented / inferred / unexplained-presumed-community) — this maps to how experts caveat opinions under §3.003(b).

One-click court exhibit export: render the chart plus schedule as a paginated PDF exhibit with case caption, Bates-style document references, and the summary-evidence foundation language (Welder), because the demo audience's end product is a trial exhibit, not a dashboard.
